title: Q01 — Is the postseason run environment (average total runs) different from the regular season?
hypothesis: Is the postseason run environment (average total runs) different from the regular season?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: 2025 PO avg total 8.02 vs 2025 REG 8.89 (delta -0.87). P1 (real scores) only; single-season sample -> directional, not conclusive.

title: Q02 — Is postseason scoring more or less volatile (std of run margin) than REG?
hypothesis: Is postseason scoring more or less volatile (std of run margin) than REG?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: 2025 PO margin std 2.22 vs 2025 REG 2.87 (delta -0.65); single season.

title: Q03 — Is home advantage larger or smaller in the postseason than in REG?
hypothesis: Is home advantage larger or smaller in the postseason than in REG?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: PO home-win 0.536 (2019-25 corpus, P1+P2 winners) vs REG 0.533 (2015-25). Directional; P2 games have no scores but known winners, sufficient for home-win frequency.

title: Q04 — Does late-season (September) form predict postseason games better than full-season strength?
hypothesis: Does late-season (September) form predict postseason games better than full-season strength?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: September-15 form on PO: 0.532 vs Elo baseline 0.539; Brier 0.3248 vs 0.2482. Late-season form adds no clear edge on PO in this sample (and calibrates poorly).

title: Q05 — Does the regular-season model transfer unchanged to the postseason (Model A)?
hypothesis: Does the regular-season model transfer unchanged to the postseason (Model A)?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Model A (REG Elo unchanged on PO): win rate 0.539 on 295 PO games (fair-coin proxy ROI +7.8%). Baseline is strong.

title: Q06 — Does REG + late-season adjustment (Model B) beat Model A on PO?
hypothesis: Does REG + late-season adjustment (Model B) beat Model A on PO?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Model B (late-season form) 0.532 vs Model A 0.539. Brier: B=0.3248 vs A=0.2482 — B's win rate similar but probabilities poorly calibrated.

title: Q07 — Does a dedicated postseason model with series state (Model C) beat Model A?
hypothesis: Does a dedicated postseason model with series state (Model C) beat Model A?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Model C (dedicated PO + series state, elimination/clinching games only) 0.542 on 83 games vs A 0.539; Brier C=0.2482. Promising on the subset it covers; sample small.

title: Q08 — Do round-specific models (Model D) outperform a single POST model, per round?
hypothesis: Do round-specific models (Model D) outperform a single POST model, per round?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Model D round-specific win rates: WC 0.583, DS 0.546, LCS 0.494, WS 0.523. Strong in WC, weak/negative in WS — round matters a lot; a single POST model is a compromise.

title: Q09 — Does the hierarchical REG-prior/PO-likelihood model (Model E) beat Model A?
hypothesis: Does the hierarchical REG-prior/PO-likelihood model (Model E) beat Model A?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Model E (hierarchical) 0.565 on 352 games vs A 0.539; Brier E=0.2614 vs A=0.2482.

title: Q10 — Is the World Series the most market-efficient / hardest round to beat?
hypothesis: Is the World Series the most market-efficient / hardest round to beat?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: WS model win rate 0.523 (fair-coin +4.5%) is the WORST round — consistent with the WS being the most efficient/hardest round. n=44 (small).

title: Q11 — Do elimination games (must-win) show a measurable performance/edge effect?
hypothesis: Do elimination games (must-win) show a measurable performance/edge effect?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Elimination/clinching games: model win rate 0.542 vs baseline 0.539 on comparable PO games. Signal positive; n=83 is small — forward-test in 2026.

title: Q12 — Do clinching games (series on the line to win) show a measurable effect?
hypothesis: Do clinching games (series on the line to win) show a measurable effect?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season

findings.note: clinching and elimination bundled in Q11 sample

conclusion: Clinching subset not separated from elimination in the current strategy; flagged for a dedicated follow-up strategy.

title: Q13 — Are Wild Card series more predictable (higher model win rate) than later rounds?
hypothesis: Are Wild Card series more predictable (higher model win rate) than later rounds?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: WC model win rate 0.583 (fair-coin +16.7%) — the most predictable round in the sample. n=48.

title: Q14 — Is there a longshot bias in REG: are strong favorites (<= -150) underpriced?
hypothesis: Is there a longshot bias in REG: are strong favorites (<= -150) underpriced?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Strong favorites (<= -150, 2019-25 real prices): win rate 0.640, ROI -2.46% on 4178 bets. No exploitable longshot-bias edge at these prices.

title: Q15 — Are REG moneyline markets efficient against naive models (2019-2025)?
hypothesis: Are REG moneyline markets efficient against naive models (2019-2025)?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: All REG moneyline strategies lose (small) at real 2019-25 prices: LO_001 -0.38%, RM_001 -0.29%, ON_001 -0.26%, RM_001 -0.64%, AS_001 -2.46% -> naive models do not beat the verified market.

title: Q16 — Can a Poisson run-rate model beat a flat 8.5 total line?
hypothesis: Can a Poisson run-rate model beat a flat 8.5 total line?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Poisson run-rate vs flat 8.5 line: ROI +1.49% on 25408 bets. CAVEAT: no verified total lines exist in the data; settled against a synthetic 8.5 @ +95 — treat as model skill vs a flat line, NOT market efficiency.

title: Q17 — Which REG form window is most predictive: 30-game, September-15, or full-season?
hypothesis: Which REG form window is most predictive: 30-game, September-15, or full-season?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: REG settled win rates: 30-game form 0.560, September-15 0.544, full-season 0.567. Full-season strength is the best REG window in this sample (September form is WORST, contradicting the prior hypothesis).

title: Q18 — Does partial pooling (REG prior + PO likelihood, shrinkage) improve PO probability calibration?
hypothesis: Does partial pooling (REG prior + PO likelihood, shrinkage) improve PO probability calibration?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Probability calibration (Brier) on PO: A=0.2482, E=0.2614. Hierarchical shrinkage did NOT improve calibration here; its edge is win-rate, not probability quality.

title: Q19 — Are 2020 bubble postseason games a distinct environment (scoring/volatility)?
hypothesis: Are 2020 bubble postseason games a distinct environment (scoring/volatility)?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: 2020 PO games are P2 (reconstructed winners, no scores) — scoring/volatility comparison impossible. Flagged, not guessed.

title: Q20 — Do rest days / travel in PO series predict game outcomes?
hypothesis: Do rest days / travel in PO series predict game outcomes?
methodology: point-in-time features, chronological walk-forward; postseason kept separate from regular season
conclusion: Rest/travel features exist in series_state (point-in-time, verified) but no strategy in v1 uses them; queued as a v2 strategy (MLB_POST_REST_001). Recorded as not-yet-tested rather than assumed.
